slides.title: Empty logs, site down
slides.tldr: A request passes through many hands before it reaches your Symfony code. If it breaks along the way, your log knows nothing about it.

blocks.body: At 11 pm customers start calling: the site won't load. Ryan logs into the server and opens `var/log/prod.log`. Not a single error. He decides the problem must be on the customers' side. In fact the requests never reached his Symfony app at all: the load balancer was turning them away with a `502` somewhere along the way. One `curl -I` from outside would have shown that 502 and who sent it.

blocks.caption: The road a request takes: what Ryan pictured vs. what really happens

columns.title: The picture in Ryan's head
items: The browser calls Symfony directly
Symfony reads the database and answers
If anything breaks, it will be in my log
columns.tip: This is what it looks like when you work on localhost, so it is the picture most CRUD developers carry around.

columns.title: The real road in production
items: The browser first looks up the address in DNS
Then it passes a CDN and a load balancer
Then Symfony, and last of all the database
If it breaks midway, Symfony's log stays empty
columns.tip: In production several separate machines sit in front of your code. Each one can break on its own.

blocks.body: Your log only sees the requests that reached your code.

aside.title: The expired domain
aside.body: One morning an organization's website vanished completely. The servers were running, the code was fine, the database was fine. The cause: nobody had paid the domain renewal fee, so DNS no longer recognized the name. For three hours everyone hunted for a bug in the code.

items.meaning: One step on a request's road: the jump from one machine to the next.
A machine in front of your app servers that spreads incoming requests across them.

check.q: The site is down, yet Symfony's log shows no errors. What does that most likely mean?
check.a: The request never reached the app. The problem is at an earlier step: DNS, the CDN or the load balancer.

slides.title: Six hops before the answer
slides.tldr: Client → DNS → CDN → load balancer → service → datastore. Each hop has its own job, and the answer comes back along the same road in reverse.

blocks.title: Going out for pizza
blocks.body: You want a pizza. First you look up the address of the pizza place: that's **DNS**. The branch at the corner keeps drinks and desserts ready-made, so you don't have to go to the main restaurant for those: that's the **CDN**. At the main restaurant's door a host sees which waiter is free and sends you to that table: that's the **load balancer**. The waiter takes your order (the **service**) and the kitchen pulls the pizza out of the oven (the **datastore**).

blocks.caption: The six hops of a request, and the answer coming back

nodes.label: Client
nodes.tip: You, the hungry customer. Your Vue app sends the request from here and waits for the answer.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.tip: The person who gives directions. It turns a name like shop.example into an IP like 203.0.113.10, and the answer is remembered for a while (the TTL).

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.tip: The corner branch. It serves ready-made things such as JS, CSS and images from a server near the user, and forwards everything else to your origin.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.tip: The host at the door. It checks which app server is healthy and free, and spreads requests across them. A gateway also checks auth and rate limits.

nodes.label: Service
nodes.tip: The waiter: the code you wrote. Only requests that get here show up in your log.

nodes.label: Datastore
nodes.tip: The oven and the pantry. The real data lives here. If it is slow, everyone in front of it ends up waiting.

edges.label: The browser asks: what is the IP of shop.example?
DNS tells it the address (the IP)
The request goes to that address and reaches the CDN first
If it is not a ready-made file, the CDN forwards it toward your origin
The load balancer picks a healthy app server
Symfony runs a query against the database
The answer walks the same road backward to the user

items.meaning: The internet's address book: it finds the IP address for a domain name.
Servers spread across many cities that serve ready-made files from near the user.
Your own main server, the one a CDN sits in front of.
A door like a load balancer, but it also handles auth, rate limits and routing.

items: Not every system has all six hops. A small app may have no CDN or load balancer, but DNS is always there.
Every connection also starts with a TLS (HTTPS) handshake. If the certificate has expired, the browser shows a red warning.

check.q: Which hops does a request pass between the client and the datastore? Say them in order.
check.a: Client → DNS (address lookup) → CDN → load balancer or gateway → service (Symfony) → datastore. The answer returns along the reverse road.

slides.title: What the user sees when each hop breaks
slides.tldr: Every hop breaks in its own way: name not found, 502/503/504, 500 or an endless spinner. The symptom tells you which hop failed.

blocks.body: If you go to a restaurant and get no food, the reason depends on where things went wrong: you never found the address, the door was locked, or the waiter says the oven is empty. Requests are the same. The error's shape carries the mark of the hop that broke, and **who sent the answer** is the biggest clue of all.

blocks.caption: Where it breaks and what it looks like

cells: No internet, or the connection drops
No response at all; fetch throws an error
rows.tip: The request never left the device. There is no status code at all: in Vue, fetch throws a TypeError.

cells: The browser says the site can't be found
rows.tip: The browser shows ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED. It happens with an expired domain or a wrong DNS record. Old answers stay cached until the TTL runs out, so not everyone breaks at the same moment.

cells: Serves stale files, or can't reach the origin
An old page, or the CDN's own error page
rows.tip: If the CDN serves cached old JS, it won't match the new API. If it can't reach the origin, it shows a 5xx page that it generates itself.
502 Bad Gateway: the server behind it refused the connection or sent back garbage. 503 Service Unavailable: there is no healthy server to send to.

cells: Your code doesn't answer in time
rows.tip: 504 Gateway Timeout: the load balancer waited as long as it was willing to and gave up. Your code may still be working on the request.
500 Internal Server Error comes from your own app. It means the request did reach your code, and the stack trace is in your log.

cells: Out of connections, or a slow query
rows.tip: The database never answers the user directly. Its failure passes through Symfony and becomes a 500 or 503, or, if it is slow, reaches the user as the load balancer's 504.

blocks.body: 502, 503 and 504 usually say: the doorman in the middle could not reach the server behind him. A 500 says: your own code broke.

aside.body: When you see a 5xx, first ask: who sent this answer, my app or someone in front of it?

items: Look at the response's `Server` and `Via` headers. They often say who answered.
One problem can look two ways: when the database is slow, some users get a 500 and others get a 504.

items.label: A timeout on every network call

check.q: A user sees 504 Gateway Timeout. Who sent that answer, and what does it mean?
check.a: The load balancer or gateway did. It waited for the app server behind it until its time limit ran out, so the app or the database is very slow.

slides.title: Spotting the broken hop in client code
slides.tldr: In the Vue client, sort failures into no response, timeout, gateway 5xx, app 5xx and your own mistake, and show a different message for each.

blocks.body: If every failure shows the same "Something went wrong", users can't tell whether to wait or to check their own internet. The client can recognize the kind of failure itself, because a break at each hop looks different to `fetch`. The small wrapper below does that sorting, and it also puts a time limit on every request.

marks.tip: Without a time limit, fetch can hang forever. AbortSignal.timeout cancels the request on its own when time is up.
fetch throws only when no response comes back at all. It does not throw on a 404 or a 500.
These three codes usually come from a load balancer or gateway, and the problem is more likely to be temporary.
The body of a gateway's 502 page is usually HTML. Calling json() first would throw a SyntaxError and hide the real cause.

blocks.caption: What to tell the user for each kind of failure

rows.tip: No response came back. Before blaming the server, the honest message is to ask users to check their own connection.

cells: This is taking longer than usual, try again
rows.tip: You don't know whether the work was done. Blindly resending a request that moves money, for example, is dangerous.

cells: A temporary problem on our side, try again shortly
rows.tip: The app server is down, a deploy is running or the load is too high. It usually clears up within seconds to minutes.

cells: Our mistake, the team has been notified
rows.tip: A bug in the code. The user can't do anything about it, and trying again will usually give the same result.
Bad input, not logged in or no permission. Show the user the reason the server sent.

aside.title: Testing hop by hop from outside

items.desc: Which IP DNS returns for this name
See the status and headers: who answered (Server, Via)
Time to DNS, connection and first byte: which hop is slow
Is the request reaching the app at all?

items: Ten seconds suits ordinary API calls. For a big upload or a report export, give that one call a longer limit instead of cutting off honest work.
Test from the outside in: DNS → CDN and load balancer → app → database. The hop after the last healthy one is the suspect.

items.label: Joining the whole road with a correlation ID

check.q: The body of a gateway's 502 response is usually HTML. What happens if the client calls `res.json()` first, and what is the right order?
check.a: JSON parsing throws a SyntaxError and hides the real cause. Check the status first, decide the kind of failure, and read the JSON only on success.

slides.title: Every user shows the same IP
slides.tldr: Behind a load balancer, Symfony can't see the real client IP or HTTPS unless you tell it, with trusted_proxies, whom to believe.

blocks.body: When a new hand joins the road, the world looks different from where your code sits. The waiter gets orders from the host, so unless he asks, he doesn't know who the real customer is. Symfony likewise sees a request that came from the load balancer's IP, over plain HTTP. The result: `getClientIp()` returns the same IP for everyone, and if you rate limit by IP, one person's misbehavior blocks everybody.

blocks.caption: Whose IP Symfony sees after the load balancer

actors.label: User
actors.tip: The real customer. Their IP is 103.4.5.6, and they are talking over HTTPS.

actors.label: Load balancer
actors.tip: HTTPS ends here. It opens a fresh connection to the app behind it, from its own IP (10.0.0.5).

actors.label: Symfony
actors.tip: It only knows the IP of whoever connected to it directly. The rest has to come from headers, and only if it is allowed to trust them.

messages.label: HTTP request, IP 10.0.0.5
messages.tip: The load balancer opens the new connection itself, so the sender address Symfony sees is the load balancer's.

messages.label: X-Forwarded-For: 103.4.5.6
messages.tip: It writes the real customer's identity into a header. X-Forwarded-Proto: https comes along with it.
By default Symfony ignores these headers, because anyone can forge a header like that.
If the load balancer's address is on the trusted list, Symfony takes the real IP from the headers it wrote.

blocks.code:
framework:
    # Only your own load balancer's address, never the whole internet
    trusted_proxies: '%env(TRUSTED_PROXIES)%'   # e.g. 10.0.0.0/8
    trusted_headers:
        - 'x-forwarded-for'      # the real client's IP
        - 'x-forwarded-proto'    # whether it was really https
        - 'x-forwarded-host'
        - 'x-forwarded-port'

marks.tip: Only requests from this IP range get their X-Forwarded-* headers believed. Headers from anyone else are ignored.
Without this, Symfony thinks the connection is HTTP. Generated links become http://, and redirects to HTTPS loop forever.

items: Don't make every IP trusted. Then anyone can set `X-Forwarded-For` themselves, pose as any IP and dodge your rate limit.
If you have both a CDN and a load balancer, both of their addresses belong on the trusted list.

items.desc: Which proxies are trusted right now

check.q: Behind a load balancer, `$request->getClientIp()` returns 10.0.0.5 for everyone. Why, and what is the fix?
check.a: Symfony sees the IP of whoever connected directly, which is the load balancer. Put the load balancer's address in `trusted_proxies` and it will take the real IP from `X-Forwarded-For`.

slides.title: One renamed field, 30,000 blank phones
slides.tldr: Many clients read your API response, known and unknown. Rename one field and the old clients quietly break.

blocks.body: Ryan renamed the API's `name` field to `fullName`, because the new name felt clearer to him. He fixed the Vue web app and deployed it the same day, and all was well. But 30,000 people still have an old version of the mobile app on their phones, and it still looks for `name`. Next morning every profile shows an empty space where the name should be, and the server logs no error at all.

blocks.caption: What the old mobile app gets after the rename

actors.label: Mobile app v1.2
actors.tip: The user hasn't updated yet. This app expects the response to contain a field called name.

actors.label: API
actors.tip: Ryan's Symfony app. He assumed only his own Vue app reads its responses.

messages.tip: In the code it looks like renaming a property, but in fact it breaks a promise made to everyone.

messages.label: 200 OK  {"fullName": "Ryan"}
messages.tip: The status is 200, so nobody sees an error.
The app may not even crash. Showing the wrong thing is more dangerous, because nobody notices.

blocks.body: An API is a promise. You can't change its shape without telling the people standing on it.
blocks.by: The first rule of API contracts

aside.title: The phone that never updates
aside.body: On the web you can ship new code to everyone within a minute. With a mobile app you can't: some people go months without updating, and a store release can sit in review. So old versions keep calling your API for a year or more.

items.meaning: The agreement, written or unwritten, between an API and its users: which URL, what to send, what comes back.
A change after which a client that used to work now misbehaves or breaks.

check.q: Ryan only renamed a property in his own code. Why did that become a big problem?
check.a: Because that name was part of the API's contract. Clients that hadn't updated still looked for the old name and found nothing.

slides.title: Which changes are safe, which break
slides.tldr: Adding something new is safe; renaming, deleting or changing a type breaks. If readers ignore fields they don't know, both sides can grow in peace.

blocks.title: The wall socket and the plug
blocks.body: For years, any appliance's plug fits the socket in your wall. You can install a new socket next to it and nothing happens to anyone. But change the size of the old socket's holes, and every appliance in the house stops working.

When the new server can still handle old clients, that is **backward compatibility**. When an older party can cope with fields it doesn't recognize from a newer one, that is **forward compatibility**. On the client side this takes the form of a tolerant reader: read only the fields you need, and look past the rest.

blocks.caption: What each change does to an old client

cells: Add a new field to the response
rows.tip: A new socket beside the old one. The old client never looks at the new field, so nothing changes for it.

cells: Add a new optional query parameter
Never sends it, works as before
rows.tip: If the default keeps the old behavior, old requests work exactly as they did.
You can't break something nobody is calling.

cells: Finds nothing under the old name
rows.tip: You can make this a safe change in steps: add the new name and keep the old one for a while.

cells: What it was looking for is gone
rows.tip: Even if nobody seems to use it, you can't remove it until you're sure.
It looks like a small change, but in typed languages (TypeScript, Kotlin) parsing the whole response can fail.

cells: Add a new required field to the request
rows.tip: Old clients don't even know the new field exists. Always make new fields optional, with a default.

blocks.body: Adding is safe. Renaming, deleting and changing a type all break.

aside.body: Be strict when you send and generous when you read: read only what you need and ignore anything unfamiliar.

items: Adding a new value to an enum is risky too: an old client may hit an unknown value and break in its switch. Tell clients to keep a default branch for unknown values.

items.label: The same rule applies to databases: expand, then contract

check.q: Why doesn't adding a new field called `phone` to an API response break old clients?
check.a: Old clients only read the fields they know. They never even look at the unknown one, so their behavior stays as before.

slides.title: Renaming safely: send both for a while
slides.tldr: To rename a field without blanking old phones, add the new name, keep the old one, wait until nobody reads it, then remove it.

blocks.body: Ryan still wants `fullName`. The safe way takes several releases instead of one. First he sends both keys, so old and new apps are both happy. Later, when nobody reads `name` any more, he deletes it.

marks.tip: One deploy, one rename. Every app that still looks for name now finds nothing, and the server logs no error.
New apps and the Vue app move to this key.
Old apps keep working. Both keys come from the same call, so they can never disagree.

blocks.caption: The safe rename, in four releases

steps.title: 1. Add the new
steps.tip: This release is purely additive, so it is safe on its own.

steps.title: 2. Move clients
steps.body: Web and new app versions read fullName
steps.tip: Ship the new client versions. Old apps still read name and keep working.

steps.title: 3. Measure
steps.body: Log how many calls come from old app versions
steps.tip: Count by the app-version header. Do not guess whether anyone still needs name.

steps.title: 4. Remove the old
steps.body: Delete name once that count is about zero
steps.tip: Only now is deleting safe. If some phones never update, ask them to update, or version the API instead.

use: Renaming or reshaping a field that clients you do not control already read
avoid: A field only your own web app reads, deployed together with the API: just rename it
A change you cannot express by adding (a type change that must replace the old shape): use a new API version

items: The price: the response is a little bigger and you carry two keys for months. Fill both from one value, or they will drift apart.

check.q: Why is sending both `name` and `fullName` safe, and when can you delete `name`?
check.a: Old apps still find `name`, new ones read `fullName`, so nobody breaks. Delete `name` only when your logs show almost no calls from old app versions.

slides.title: When you must break: which versioning method
slides.tldr: If you can't avoid a break, ship a new version. The simplest and most common method is /v1, /v2 in the URL. The real work is keeping one set of logic under both versions.

blocks.body: Not every change can be made by adding. Sometimes the shape really has to change. When that happens, keep the old socket and install a second one with the new holes. There are four common ways to tell the sockets apart.

blocks.caption: Four ways to version an API

rows.tip: The default for most teams. In logs, curl and the browser you can see the version at a glance, and routing and caching stay simple.

cells: Hard to see, caches need Vary
rows.tip: It's elegant from a pure REST point of view, but you can't just open it in a browser, and testing it is a hassle.

cells: Easy to forget, muddles cache keys
rows.tip: If the parameter is left out, it is unclear which version the caller gets. That is why this one is less popular.

cells: Small changes are easy to handle
rows.tip: Each client stays pinned to its own date. Stripe does it this way, but the server has to remember what changed on every date.

blocks.code:
api_v1:
    resource: ../src/Controller/Api/V1/
    type: attribute
    prefix: /api/v1

api_v2:
    resource: ../src/Controller/Api/V2/
    type: attribute
    prefix: /api/v2

marks.tip: Every controller in the V1 folder gets a route starting with /api/v1. You don't repeat the prefix in each controller.
V2 sits right beside it. Both controllers call the same application service; only the shape of the response differs.
Both versions call the same service. A bug fixed in the business rules is fixed once, for everybody.
Only the outside differs: v1 keeps price as the string "12.50", v2 sends whole cents as a number.

blocks.body: A new version doesn't mean a new house. The logic under both versions stays the same; only the outside looks different.

use: URL version: public APIs, mobile apps and partners, where you don't control the clients
No version at all: only your own Vue app calls it, and both sides deploy together
avoid: A new version for every small change: you end up running ten versions at once

items: Keep the number of versions low. Running more than two at once is usually a burden on the team.
Bump the major version (v1, v2) only for a real break. Additive changes can go into any version quietly.
The price of versions: every extra one needs its own tests and its own docs until it is retired.

check.q: What is the best way to cut the extra maintenance when you run two versions side by side?
check.a: Give each version its own controller, but share the application service underneath. Then there is one set of business rules and only the response shape comes in two forms.

slides.title: A safe way to retire an old version
slides.tldr: Never switch it off suddenly. Announce it, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, measure who still uses it, and shut it down only when the date arrives.

blocks.body: When a train timetable changes, notices go up at the stations well in advance; the trains don't just stop. Retiring an old API version works the same way. Put a header on every response saying that this version is old and when it will end, then watch whether anyone is still calling it.

blocks.caption: Five steps to retire an old version

steps.title: 1. Announce
steps.body: The new version is ready; give the shutdown date early
steps.tip: Announce it by email, in the changelog and in the docs together. Pick a date that gives mobile clients time to update, usually a few months.

steps.title: 2. Send headers
steps.body: Deprecation and Sunset on every old response
steps.tip: A client whose code reads these headers can show a warning by itself. It is an announcement that needs no human.

steps.title: 3. Measure usage
steps.body: Log which clients still call v1
steps.tip: Count by client name or app-version header. As the date gets closer, the number should head toward zero.

steps.title: 4. Tell them directly
steps.body: Contact those who still call it, one by one
steps.tip: Phone or email the big partners. Not everyone reads the changelog.

steps.title: 5. Shut it down
steps.tip: 410 says "this existed and is gone". It is clearer than a 404, because the client knows the URL is not a mistake.

marks.tip: Runs only for v1 URLs. v2 responses are left untouched.
The Deprecation header carries the date the version was declared old, as a Unix timestamp with a leading @.
Sunset is the shutdown date, in HTTP date format. After it, v1 will be gone.

items.desc: Whether the response headers carry Deprecation and Sunset

items: A week or two before shutdown you can run a "brownout": deliberately return 410 from v1 for a few set hours, so anyone still calling it suddenly notices.

items.label: Which hop of the request path can change headers

check.q: Why do you need headers and usage measurement on top of announcing the v1 shutdown date by email?
check.a: Not everyone reads the email. Headers tell clients in code, and measuring shows who will break if you shut it down.

slides.title: The test that changes along with the code
slides.tldr: The developer who changes a field also changes the test, so the break goes unnoticed. A contract test guards, separately, what old clients rely on.

blocks.body: Ryan renamed `name` to `fullName` and changed the test line `assertSame('Ryan', $data['name'])` in the same commit. Everything stays green. Here the test speaks for the change, not for the clients who depend on the API. A contract test stores, in a separate place, exactly what old clients expect, so that changing it forces everyone to ask questions.

marks.tip: This comment records who relies on it. If you want to change the test, you first have to talk to that client.
It only checks that the key exists and the type matches. It doesn't match the exact values of the whole response, which would be brittle.

blocks.caption: A consumer-driven contract: from the client's expectations to the API's CI

nodes.label: Client team
nodes.tip: The people who use the response. They are the ones who know which fields are really needed.

nodes.label: Contract file
nodes.tip: The client's expectations written in one file: which URL it calls and which fields it expects. Pact does this job.

nodes.label: API CI
nodes.tip: On every change it runs the real API against this file.

nodes.label: Deploy
nodes.tip: If the check fails, the change never gets here. The break is caught before it reaches production.

edges.label: The client team writes its expectations into a file
The API's CI pulls in that file
The deploy goes ahead only if the expectations match

items.desc: Compares two OpenAPI files and finds breaking changes

items.meaning: The client that uses the API writes down what it expects from it, and the API verifies exactly that.
A popular tool for consumer-driven contract tests; it works with both PHP and JS.

aside.body: Check your own change with your own tests, but check other people's reliance with expectations written by them.

check.q: If the same developer can change the response and the test, how is a contract test different?
check.a: A contract test pins the old client's expectations in a separate place. Changing the response turns it red, and everyone notices.

slides.title: One phone screen, five requests
slides.tldr: No single API style fits every job. On a small mobile screen you sometimes get far more data than you need, and sometimes have to call again and again for one screen.

blocks.body: The profile screen in Ryan's mobile app needs only a name, a photo and the last three orders. But `GET /api/users/7` returns 40 fields, most of which the screen never uses. To get the orders he has to make more separate requests. On a slow mobile network, every extra round trip means more waiting.

actors.tip: It wants to show the profile screen: name, photo, last three orders.

actors.label: REST API

aside.body: One API serves the web, mobile and partners. The three need three different things, but there is only one shape.
