Getting more data than you need.
Not getting enough data in one go, so you have to call again and again.

check.q: A mobile screen needs 5 separate requests to show a profile. What kind of problem is that, and why is it bad?
check.a: It is under-fetching. Every request costs a network round trip, so on a slow network the screen takes a long time to draw.

slides.title: Four ways to order food
slides.tldr: REST is a fixed menu, GraphQL is building your own plate, gRPC is a walkie-talkie to the kitchen, and a message is leaving a note: four styles, four different strengths.

blocks.title: Ordering at a restaurant
blocks.body: **REST** is the printed menu: every item has a name and a price, and you get what is listed. **GraphQL** is building your own plate: "a little rice, two pieces of fish, no dal", all in one order. **gRPC** is the walkie-talkie between the waiter and the kitchen, coded in advance: fast, but a customer from outside doesn't speak that language. A **message** is leaving a note: the customer doesn't stand waiting for an answer, and gets called when the food is ready.

blocks.caption: The strength and the price of each of the four styles

cells: Too much or too little data
rows.tip: Everybody knows it, and HTTP caching and tooling are the most mature. The default choice for most APIs.

cells: One endpoint, the client writes a query
rows.tip: The client says which fields it wants, so over-fetching and repeated calls go down. In exchange, the server gets more complex.
Fast, with precise types, but a browser can't speak gRPC directly: you need gRPC-Web or a proxy in between.

cells: A message in a queue or broker
rows.tip: The client moves on without waiting. To learn the result, it checks a status later or listens for an event signal.

blocks.body: Default to REST. The other three are cures for specific pains, not everyday food.

aside.body: Menu (REST), your own plate (GraphQL), walkie-talkie (gRPC), note (message).

items.meaning: The compact binary format gRPC sends data in; the shape is written in a .proto file.
A newer version of HTTP in which many requests share one connection at the same time.

check.q: Of the four, which is the easiest to call directly from a Vue app running in a browser, and which is not direct?
check.a: REST (and GraphQL) work over HTTP and JSON, so a browser can call them directly. gRPC can't run straight from a browser: you need gRPC-Web or a proxy.

slides.title: What GraphQL and gRPC look like
slides.tldr: In GraphQL the client writes exactly what it wants and fetches it in one go. In gRPC the .proto file is the contract, and a field's number can never change.

blocks.body: The profile screen from the first story takes just one request in GraphQL: the client writes which fields it wants. In gRPC the shape lives in a `.proto` file, and both sides generate their own code from it. Look at the two side by side.

marks.tip: Only these two fields come back. Not 40: over-fetching is gone.
The user and their last 3 orders in the same request. No separate round trip needed.
Typed code is generated from this service for both client and server. Send the wrong type and the compiler catches it.
= 2 is the field number. This number goes over the wire, not the name. So changing the number is a breaking change.

blocks.caption: The same screen, REST vs. GraphQL

columns.title: REST
items: 5 separate requests
The full shape of each resource
URL-based HTTP caching is easy
columns.tip: A separate URL for each resource. The simplest approach, but when a screen gets complex you have to call again and again.

columns.title: GraphQL
items: 1 request
Only the requested fields
Usually all POST, so caching is hard
columns.tip: The client writes the shape it needs. The server returns only that.

items: In GraphQL a client can write a query as deep or as heavy as it likes. Without depth and cost limits, a single query can bring the server down.
If every nested field goes to the database separately, you get N+1. Plan a batching technique (DataLoader) ahead of time.

check.q: In protobuf, why can't the `= 2` in `int64 total_cents = 2;` be changed?
check.a: That number is what identifies the field on the wire. If you change it, old clients read a different field, so it is a breaking change.

slides.title: The pain gRPC cures: a renamed field
slides.tldr: Between two internal services, hand-written JSON drifts apart without a sound. A shared .proto turns the same rename into a loud failure before deploy.

blocks.body: Ryan's order service asks the payment service, run by another team, for an order's total. The reply is hand-written JSON. On Tuesday the payment team renames `total` to `total_cents`. Nothing crashes: the order service reads a key that no longer exists, gets nothing, and quietly shows $0 on every order until a customer complains.

blocks.title: The kitchen's code list
blocks.body: The waiter and the kitchen talk by walkie-talkie in codes: "7" means pizza. If the kitchen changes what 7 means and tells nobody, the waiter keeps shouting 7 and wrong plates keep coming out. A `.proto` file is one printed code list that both sides must generate from, so a changed code shows up before the first order.

blocks.code:
$data = $this->http
    ->request('GET', 'http://payments.internal/orders/'.$id)
    ->toArray();

$total = $data['total'] ?? 0;   // renamed upstream: silently 0 now

marks.tip: A missing array key is not an error in PHP. The ?? 0 even hides it, so the wrong number flows on.
A failed call comes back as a status you must look at, not as a quietly empty result.
After the .proto changes and the code is regenerated, this method is gone. Static analysis in CI flags it, and in Go or Java the build stops.

blocks.caption: What gRPC fixes between internal services, and what it costs

columns.title: What it fixes
items: One .proto file is the contract; both sides generate code from it
A rename fails in CI, not in production
Small on the wire: 35 bytes of JSON for an order, about 12 in Protobuf
columns.tip: The pain is two teams changing a shared shape without noticing. A generated contract makes the change visible to both sides.

columns.title: What it costs
items: Every build needs protoc and the gRPC PHP extension
Bodies are binary: curl and log files show noise
Not for browsers or outside partners
columns.tip: You pay in tooling and in how hard it is to look at traffic. For a few calls between two services of one team, that price is not worth it.

use: Many calls between services you own, possibly in more than one language
avoid: One team, one app, a few calls: REST with an OpenAPI file is enough
Clients you do not control, such as browsers and partners

items.meaning: The tool that reads a .proto file and writes the client and server code for your language.

check.q: Payment renames `total` in its JSON. Why does the order service fail silently, and why does the gRPC version fail early?
check.a: A missing array key just gives nothing, and `?? 0` hides it. With gRPC the field is a generated method, so after regeneration the old name no longer exists and CI catches it.

slides.title: The style that doesn't make you wait: 202 Accepted
slides.tldr: For slow work, take the request, answer at once with 202 and a status URL; a Messenger worker does the job in the background and the client asks later.

blocks.body: Say a monthly report takes 20 seconds to build. Making the user sit for 20 seconds risks a timeout as well. The note-leaving style does it differently: the API puts the job on a queue and immediately answers `202 Accepted`, along with a URL where the report's status can be checked. The client asks that URL now and then.

blocks.caption: Building a report: leave a note, check back later

actors.label: Vue app
actors.tip: It asked for a report, but doesn't sit there blocked.

actors.label: API
actors.tip: It only puts the job on the queue and hands back a receipt. It doesn't do the heavy work itself.

actors.label: Worker
actors.tip: It sits in the background, picks jobs off the queue and builds the report.

messages.label: 202 Accepted, Location: /reports/9
messages.tip: The receipt: the job has been accepted but not finished. Location is the address where you can look at that receipt.

messages.note: Building the report in the background

marks.tip: First a report row in the database, with status pending. The client needs something real to be pointed at.
dispatch only puts the message on the queue. The heavy work runs in the GenerateReport handler, inside the worker.
202 means accepted, work not finished yet. Answering 200 or 201 would make the client think the report exists.

items.desc: Start a worker to pick up jobs from the queue

items: When the status endpoint says done, give the result URL, and when it says failed, give the reason. With only pending and done, a failed job stays "pending" forever.
Leave two or three seconds between polls. Calling every 100ms puts load on your own API.

check.q: Why return `202 Accepted` instead of `200 OK` for slow work?
check.a: 200 makes the client think the work is finished. 202 says honestly: the work was accepted but isn't done, check the Location URL for the result.

slides.title: Which one, and when: a decision chart
slides.tldr: Choose by situation: REST for public and ordinary work, GraphQL for complex screens across many clients, gRPC between internal services, messages for slow work.

blocks.body: The question when picking a style isn't "which one is modern?" but "where does it hurt?". Where nothing hurts, a new style only adds complexity. The chart below points to the straight path by situation.

blocks.caption: Choosing a style by situation

cells: An outside partner or a public API
rows.tip: Everyone knows it, you can try it with curl, and caching and tooling are mature.

cells: A plain CRUD app from one team
rows.tip: Nothing hurts, so the straight path is best. Learning and running another style is cost for no reason.

cells: Web, mobile, TV: many clients, different screens
rows.tip: Each client wants the shape it needs. Otherwise you would have to build a separate endpoint for each.

cells: Your own internal services, lots of calls, speed matters
rows.tip: You control both sides, so sharing the .proto file is easy. The binary format gives extra speed.

cells: Slow work that can happen later
rows.tip: There is no need to keep the user waiting. The queue holds the work and a worker does it later.

cells: One event many parties will hear (an order was placed)
rows.tip: The sender doesn't even know who is listening. Adding a new listener doesn't change the sender's code.

blocks.title: Ask before you pick a style
items: Does the pain really exist, or do you just feel like trying something new?
Who are the clients: your own, or unknown people outside?
Does anyone on the team know how to run and fix it?
Does the user need the answer right now?

blocks.body: Mixing styles in one system is fine: REST outside, gRPC inside, messages for slow work.

use: GraphQL: when you have many kinds of clients and screens that change often
gRPC: when both sides are yours, and you need speed and a typed contract
avoid: GraphQL: in a small CRUD app, just because it is "modern"
gRPC: when handing an API directly to outside partners, especially browser clients

items.label: Whatever the style, protect the contract

check.q: A small app with one Vue frontend and one Symfony backend. What should you ask yourself before bringing in GraphQL?
check.a: Where does it hurt, and does it hurt at all? With a single client there is almost no over-fetching or repeated-call problem, so plain REST is enough.

slides.title: Page 5000 takes 3 seconds
slides.tldr: Paginating with OFFSET gets slower the deeper you go, and when new data arrives the pages shift, so rows go missing or show up twice.

blocks.body: Ryan's admin panel has 1 million orders, 20 per page. He wrote `LIMIT 20 OFFSET :page * 20`, and the first few pages were instant. But when the auditor opened page 5000, the query took about 3 seconds. The reason: with an OFFSET of 100,000 (5,000 pages of 20), the database first counts and throws away 100,000 rows, and only then hands over the 20.

blocks.caption: Example: how OFFSET query time grows with the page number (table of 1 million rows)

items.label: Page 1
items.tip: The first page has almost nothing to skip. That is why everything feels fast in testing.

items.label: Page 100
items.tip: It skips about 2,000 rows and then takes 20.

items.label: Page 1000
items.tip: It reads and discards about 20,000 rows. The time grows in a straight line with the page number.

items.label: Page 5000
items.tip: It reads and discards about 100,000 rows just to keep 20.

blocks.body: OFFSET N means: the database reads N rows, throws them away, then gives you yours. The deeper the page, the higher the cost.

aside.title: The second danger: pages that shift
aside.body: Kevin looked at page 1 and then clicked page 2, but in between 5 new orders came in. Every old row moved down by 5 places, so the last 5 orders of page 1 showed up again at the top of page 2. The other way around, if rows are deleted, some rows are skipped entirely.

items.meaning: Splitting a big list into small pages and serving it a little at a time.
The number of rows to skip from the start before you begin reading.

check.q: Why is fetching a page with OFFSET 100000 slow, when only 20 rows come back?
check.a: The database has to get through the first 100,000 rows and discard them before it returns 20. The cost matches the rows skipped, not the rows returned.

slides.title: A bookmark: start after the last row
slides.tldr: Cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the value of the last row you saw and asks for "the 20 after that one". The index jumps straight there, so every page is equally fast.

blocks.title: A library book and a bookmark
blocks.body: If someone says "keep reading after page 500" in a thick book, you won't count 500 pages from the start. You open it at the bookmark. Offset is counting pages, and a cursor is the bookmark. The last row is the bookmark: "give me the 20 after this row".

blocks.caption: Offset vs. cursor: the same list of 1 million rows

columns.title: Offset pagination
items: Deep pages are slow: all the OFFSET rows must be read
New rows shift the pages: rows go missing or repeat
"Jump to page 50" is easy
columns.tip: Works by page number. Simple, but slow and unstable on big lists.

columns.title: Cursor (keyset)
items: Every page is equally fast, the index goes straight to the spot
New rows don't shift the pages
"Next" and "previous" are easy, "jump to page 50" is not
columns.tip: Works from the value of the last row. The right way for big lists that change often.

blocks.title: The three parts of a cursor
items: The cursor is the sort value of the last row, such as created_at and id.
The query says: give me the rows "after" this value.
The response carries `nextCursor`; the client sends it back to get the next page.

use: Cursor: infinite scroll, feeds, logs, big or frequently changing lists, public APIs
Offset: small, stable tables (a few hundred rows) where you really need "jump to page 5"
avoid: Offset on a list of millions of rows

items: Running COUNT(*) on a big table to show the total number of pages is slow as well. Cursor APIs usually just say whether there is more.

aside.body: Don't count your way there, keep a bookmark.

check.q: Why does a cursor query run at the same speed on page 1 or page 5000?
check.a: Because the database skips no rows. From the index it goes straight to the last row you saw and picks up 20.

slides.title: A keyset query in Doctrine
slides.tldr: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC, and the next-page condition (created_at < :at) OR (created_at = :at AND id < :id). Fetch one extra row to learn whether there is more.

blocks.body: We keep two values in the cursor: `createdAt` and `id`. We hand it to the client as an opaque string, so the client doesn't break if the internal structure changes. The query has one trick: we fetch `limit + 1` rows, and if the extra row shows up, we know there are more pages.

marks.tip: URL-safe base64 (+ and / replaced with - and _). The client sends it back as a meaningless string.
Return a 400 for a broken or forged cursor, never a 500. It is user input.
When created_at is equal, id settles the order. Without it, rows with the same timestamp can go missing (see the last slide).
limit + 1: if the extra row arrives, there is a next page. That is far cheaper than a separate COUNT query.
DQL can't compare tuples, so the condition is spelled out with OR. The result is the same.

items: If you sort by something else (say price), put that column in the cursor too, and build an index on that column plus id.
Always enforce an upper bound on `limit` (say 100) on the server. Even if a client asks for a million, don't give it.
Doctrine's datetime columns hold whole seconds, so DATE_ATOM is enough. If you store microseconds, encode them too (`Y-m-d\TH:i:s.uP`), or rows are lost.

check.q: Why fetch `limit + 1` rows instead of `limit`?
check.a: If the extra row arrives, there is a next page (and we drop that row). That saves a separate, slow COUNT query.

slides.title: From controller to Vue: passing the cursor along
slides.tldr: The controller returns items and nextCursor. Vue sends that nextCursor back as after in the next request, and stops when it gets null.

blocks.body: The response has two things: the page's `items`, and `nextCursor`, which is `null` on the last page. The Vue app doesn't try to open the cursor and understand it. It just passes it along.

marks.tip: Whatever the client asks for, the value is clamped to between 1 and 100.
An extra row means there is a next page. Then it is cut off and never goes to the client.
On the last page nextCursor is null. The client reads that null as "no more".

blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'

type Order = { id: number; total: number }
type Page = { items: Order[]; nextCursor: string | null }

const orders = ref<Order[]>([])
const nextCursor = ref<string | null>(null)
const done = ref(false)
const loading = ref(false)

async function loadMore() {
  if (loading.value || done.value) return
  loading.value = true
  try {
    const qs = new URLSearchParams({ limit: '20' })
    if (nextCursor.value) qs.set('after', nextCursor.value)
    const res = await fetch(`/api/v1/orders?${qs}`)
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`)
    const page: Page = await res.json()
    orders.value.push(...page.items)
    nextCursor.value = page.nextCursor
    done.value = page.nextCursor === null
  } finally {
    loading.value = false
  }
}
loadMore()
</script>

marks.tip: The loading flag stops a quick double click from fetching the same page twice.
The previous page's nextCursor is this request's after. The client never opens the cursor.
When null arrives, done = true and no more requests go out.

items: For infinite scroll in Vue, call loadMore() with an IntersectionObserver when the user reaches the end of the list.
Pick one convention, a `Link` header or a `nextCursor` field, and keep it. Don't mix two styles in the same API.

items.label: Why a cursor's structure is not part of the contract

check.q: Why does the Vue app just pass the cursor string along instead of opening it up to understand it?
check.a: The cursor's internal structure is the server's business. If the client never opens it, the server can change that structure later without breaking the client.

slides.title: When rows with the same timestamp vanish
slides.tldr: If the cursor is built on created_at alone, rows from the same second get lost at the page boundary. Add a unique tie-breaker (id) to the ordering.

blocks.body: Say three orders came in together at 10:00:00. The page boundary falls right in the middle of them. The cursor now says `created_at < 10:00:00`, and the other two orders with the same time will never satisfy that condition. Rows vanish silently, with no error.

blocks.caption: The same page boundary, with and without id as a tie-breaker

rows.tip: The cursor holds this row's created_at, and with the fix its id too: (10:00:00, 105).
created_at < 10:00:00 is false for an equal time, so it is skipped. Compared as the pair, (10:00:00, 104) < (10:00:00, 105) is true.
Skipped for the same reason, and nobody notices because no error appears. The pair comparison keeps it.
With only created_at, page 2 looks perfectly normal: it simply starts two rows too late.

blocks.code:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at < :last_created_at
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

marks.tip: Rows with an equal created_at are dropped. The order isn't unique either, so the same row's position can change between two requests.
A row-value comparison: the (created_at, id) pair is compared as a unit. It works in both PostgreSQL and MySQL.
An index matching the ORDER BY. Without it you lose the speed advantage of keyset.

items: If the sort column isn't unique (created_at alone, price alone), a cursor on that order will go wrong. Always add id at the end.
If you mix ASC and DESC in the sort, the row-value comparison goes the wrong way. Keep the same direction on every column.

aside.body: A cursor's ordering must be unique: id goes last.

items.label: What your ID choice means (UUIDv7 keeps its order)

check.q: Why do some rows from the same second get lost when the cursor uses only created_at, and what is the fix?
check.a: The condition `created_at < last value` drops rows with an equal value. Add the unique id to the ordering and compare the (created_at, id) pair, and no row is lost.

slides.title: "Something went wrong"
slides.tldr: If every error is a meaningless message, or hidden inside a 200 OK, the client can do nothing: not fix it, not retry, not even stop.

blocks.body: When Ryan's API gets a bad email, it returns `200 OK` with `{"success": false, "msg": "error"}`, and when the server breaks it returns a `500` with a long stack trace. The Vue app shows "Something went wrong" in every case. The user can't tell whether to fix the email or just wait. Worse, the app sometimes resends the bad email three times, as if sending it again would make the email valid.

blocks.caption: Two kinds of answer to the same bad email

columns.title: Ryan's useless error
items: Status 200, yet the job wasn't done
Message: "error" (what is wrong, which field?)
A stack trace leaks when the server breaks
The client can't tell whether to retry
columns.tip: Neither a machine nor a person can do anything with this answer.

columns.title: A useful error
items: Status 422: the input is wrong
Which field and why: email_invalid
Server internals stay inside
The client knows: resending won't help
columns.tip: Status, reason and code together tell the client what to do next.

blocks.body: An error is the API telling the user and the client: what is wrong, whose fault it is, and what to do now.

aside.title: Failure inside a 200 OK
aside.body: A banking app returned 200 even for failed transactions, with "failed" written inside. Monitoring counted only 5xx, so the dashboard stayed green while users' money was stuck. When a status code lies, every tool (cache, monitoring, retry) goes the wrong way.

items.meaning: The three-digit number in a response that says how the job went: 2xx success, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the server's mistake.

check.q: If a failed job returns 200 OK with success: false in the body, which tools go the wrong way?
check.a: Monitoring, caching and retry policy, because they all go by the status code. Seeing 200, they assume everything is fine.

slides.title: Status codes, like a courier's return slip
slides.tldr: 2xx is success, 4xx is your (the client's) mistake, 5xx is our (the server's) mistake. Each code says whose fault it is, and whether sending again can help.

blocks.title: A courier's return slip
blocks.body: When a courier returns a parcel, the slip gives the reason. "Wrong address" means sending it again is pointless until you fix the address. "Nobody home" means trying again may work. "Problem at our warehouse" means the fault is the courier's, so try again a bit later.

blocks.caption: The most useful status codes and what they mean

cells: The input is wrong or incomplete
rows.tip: 400: the request could not be understood at all (broken JSON). 422: it was understood, but the values are not acceptable (a bad email). Sending again without fixing it is pointless.

cells: I don't know who you are (not logged in)
rows.tip: No token, or the token has expired. You can try once after renewing the token.

cells: I know who you are, but you have no permission
rows.tip: You are logged in, but this action isn't for you. Sending again changes nothing.
A wrong URL or something that was deleted. For security reasons a 404 is often used in place of a 403 too.
For example the stock ran out, or someone else changed it first. The client has to look at the new state and decide.
The rate limit was exceeded. Look at the Retry-After header and try again a little later.

cells: A problem with the server or a machine in front of it
rows.tip: There is nothing for the client to do. 502/503/504 are usually temporary, so retrying is fine.

blocks.body: A server mistake is 5xx, a client mistake is 4xx. The status itself says whose fault it is.

items: 404 or 403 for someone else's order? A 403 tells a stranger the order exists; a 404 hides it. For private data, prefer 404.
A 400 for every mistake, or a 500 for every mistake: the client then can't tell what kind of mistake it was.

check.q: A user is logged in but tries to open someone else's order. 401 or 403, and why?
check.a: 403. The server knows who they are (so not 401), but they have no permission for this action. Many APIs also return 404 to hide that the order exists.

slides.title: One error shape everybody knows: problem+json
slides.tldr: Return every error in one mould, the application/problem+json shape from RFC 9457: type, title, status, detail, plus your own machine-readable code.

blocks.body: This time Ryan decided that every error would go out in the same mould. There is a standard shape for it: **problem+json**. Alongside `status`, `title` and `detail` it carries a `code`, which the client's code reads. People read `detail` (the message can change), and code reads `code` (it never changes).

blocks.caption: The path from an exception to problem+json

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.tip: When a business rule is broken it throws its own exception, such as InsufficientStockException. It doesn't think about HTTP here.

nodes.label: ExceptionListener
nodes.tip: It catches every exception in one place and decides the status and code. Otherwise each controller invents its own errors.

nodes.label: Vue app
nodes.tip: It decides from the code, not the message, which screen or which correction to show.

edges.label: 409 + application/problem+json
edges.tip: The status gives the kind, and the code in the body gives the exact reason.

marks.tip: Symfony's own logger runs at priority 0. Running after it (-10) means a 500 is still written to the log, even though the client sees only a generic message.
When #[MapRequestPayload] validation fails, Symfony throws an HttpException whose previous is a ValidationFailedException.
This picks the status and a fixed code from our own exception. This is what the client reads.
For a 5xx the real message is not given to the client. A leaked stack trace or SQL helps an attacker.

blocks.code:
{
  "type": "https://shop.example/problems/stock_insufficient",
  "title": "Conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "code": "stock_insufficient",
  "detail": "Only 2 in stock, 5 requested"
}

marks.tip: The client decides from this code. Even if the detail's language or wording changes, the code stays the same.

items: Keep error codes short, English, snake_case and permanent: stock_insufficient. They are part of the API contract, and once given they can't be changed.
Put a request id in every error response, so a user's complaint can be matched to your log.

items.label: Error codes are part of the contract too

check.q: Why should client code decide by the `code` field and not the `detail` message?
check.a: detail is for people, and its language or wording can change. code is fixed and part of the contract, so client code can depend on it.

slides.title: Validation errors: what is wrong in which field
slides.tldr: Return all the mistakes in a form at once, each with its field, a machine-readable code and a message, so the client can show the right error beside each input.

blocks.body: On a registration form the email is wrong and the password is too short. If you return only the first mistake, the user fixes it, sends again and gets stuck on the second. So put all the mistakes together in an `errors` list, each with its `field` and a fixed `code`.

marks.tip: The fixed code goes in the payload. The message can change when the language changes, the code can't.
There is a default value, so even if the field doesn't arrive at all, you get a validation error, not a PHP type error.
The name of the field with the mistake. The client uses it to put the message beside the right input.
The fixed code from the DTO's payload, or a generic invalid if there is none.

blocks.caption: The errors list of a 422 for a bad email and a short password

rows.tip: The client sees this code, shows a red message under the email input and focuses it.
The second mistake is in the same response, so the user doesn't have to keep coming back.

items: Don't leak extra information in a message like "wrong password" or "email not registered": it lets an attacker work out which emails exist.
Even with validation in the client, validation on the server is mandatory. Client validation is only a convenience for the user.

items.label: The real reason for input validation

check.q: Why is it better to return all the mistakes in the `errors` list instead of just the first one?
check.a: The user can see and fix all the mistakes in one go. Otherwise they fix one, resend, and repeat, which is annoying.

slides.title: Blind retry: charged twice
slides.tldr: Retry only errors that are temporary, and only work that does no harm if done twice. GET, PUT and DELETE are safe; POST isn't, unless there is an idempotency key.

blocks.body: A call to the payment endpoint `POST /payments` times out. The app decides it "failed", sends it again, and the user's money is charged twice. A timeout doesn't mean the job wasn't done, it means no answer arrived. If the job is **idempotent** (doing it again and again gives the same result), sending again is safe, otherwise not.

blocks.caption: Which events deserve a retry

cells: Unknown whether the job was done
rows.tip: No answer doesn't mean it wasn't done. Safe for GET, PUT and DELETE. For POST, not without an idempotency key.
The server itself says how long to hold off. Sending before that only makes the wait longer.
With a 504 the job may already have been done, so this retry too is safe only for idempotent work.

cells: A bug gives the same result
rows.tip: If there is a bug in the code, the same request fails the same way every time. Try once at most.
Sending again without fixing the input gets the same answer. It only adds load on the server.
With a 401 you can try once after renewing the token, but sending again doesn't change the others.

marks.tip: First decide whether doing the job twice does harm. If it does, there is no need to look at anything else.
Retry only when no response arrived (network, timeout) or the status is temporary. Never for 400 or 422.

blocks.body: Retry only on temporary errors, and only for work that does no harm if done twice.

items.meaning: Repeating the same request gives the same result as doing it once. For example DELETE /orders/5.
A unique mark made by the client, which lets the server avoid doing the same job twice.

items.label: Making POST safe with an idempotency key

check.q: What is the risk if the app simply resends after a timeout on POST /payments, and how do you make it safe?
check.a: A timeout doesn't mean the job wasn't done, only that no answer arrived, so the money may be charged twice. With an idempotency key the server won't do the same job a second time.

slides.title: The fix: the same key on every retry
slides.tldr: The client makes one Idempotency-Key per user action and reuses it on every retry. The server runs the job once per key and replays the saved answer.

blocks.body: Back to the timed-out payment. The trouble was that the server could not tell "a second attempt at the same payment" from "a brand-new payment". A key fixes that: it is a label, like a token number at a bank counter, that the client makes once and sends again on each retry. The server charges once per key.

blocks.caption: A retry that does not charge twice

actors.label: Vue app
actors.tip: It made one key for this payment and keeps it for every retry of that payment.

actors.label: Payments API
actors.tip: It remembers which keys it has already handled and what it answered.

messages.note: Charges $25, saves the answer under k-77
messages.tip: The charge and the saved answer belong together: the next request with k-77 will find them.
The client cannot know whether the charge happened. This is the exact moment a blind retry would hurt.

messages.label: 201 with the first answer, no second charge
messages.tip: The server sees a key it has handled and replays the saved answer instead of running the job again.

marks.tip: If the key were made inside the loop, every retry would look like a new payment and the fix would do nothing.
The same key travels with every attempt.
cache->get() runs the callback only when the key is not saved yet. A retry gets the saved array back.
The money moves here, once per key. If it throws, nothing is saved, so a later retry may run it again.

items: Use a shared cache (Redis), not a per-server one, or a retry that lands on another server charges again.
Reject a reused key that arrives with a different body: it is a client bug, not a retry.

use: Any POST that moves money or creates something you cannot cheaply undo
avoid: GET, PUT and DELETE: they are already safe to repeat, so a key only adds storage

check.q: Why must the client create the idempotency key once per payment, and not once per attempt?
check.a: The key is how the server recognizes a retry. A fresh key on each attempt makes every retry look like a new payment, so the double charge comes back.

slides.title: One person's loop slows the site for everyone
slides.tldr: When one client (a buggy loop, a scraper, a malicious bot) fires thousands of requests, everyone else's answers slow down. With no limit, one mistake can take the whole API down.

blocks.body: A script at one of Ryan's partner companies accidentally got a `while(true)` loop, and it started calling Ryan's API 30 times a second. Each call held a database connection for about a second, and the pool had only a few dozen, so within minutes none were left and ordinary users' pages wouldn't open even after 30 seconds. Nobody attacked anything: one person's mistake hurt everybody. The fix is a per-client cap, shown in the last bar.

blocks.caption: Requests per minute by client (example)

items.label: User A
items.tip: An ordinary user, making a handful of requests a minute.

items.label: User B
items.tip: Another ordinary user. Both are far below any limit.

items.label: User C
items.tip: Even fewer. All of these are just going about their work.

items.label: Partner's loop
items.tip: Because of the buggy loop, this one client alone is about 50 times the three users' combined load (35 a minute).

items.label: Same loop, 100/min limit
items.tip: The same loop with a per-client limit: 100 requests get through each minute and the rest are refused with a 429. The three users above never notice.

blocks.body: An API without limits leaves its door open to everyone, so one person's mistake or bad faith hurts all.

aside.body: One client must not be able to eat all of the server's capacity by itself. A limit exists to stop that one client so the others stay fine.

items.meaning: The cap on how many requests one client may make in a given period of time.
The total allowance of use over a day or a month. For example 100,000 requests a month.

check.q: Why do you need a rate limit even when nobody is attacking you?
check.a: A buggy loop can fire huge numbers of requests too. You need a limit so that one person's mistake doesn't slow the service for everyone else.

slides.title: The food truck's ready plates: token bucket
slides.tldr: Token bucket: tokens collect in a bucket over time, each request spends one, and when the bucket is empty you wait. Short bursts pass, sustained pressure is stopped.

blocks.title: The food truck's ready plates
blocks.body: A taco food truck prepares 10 plates a minute, and the counter has room for at most 20 ready plates. A customer takes one plate. When a crowd suddenly turns up, the 20 saved plates go out at once (a burst), but after that only 10 a minute. If no plate is ready, it is "wait a little".

blocks.caption: Comparing three common methods

cells: At most 100 per minute, reset to zero at the end of the minute
Twice the limit gets through at the boundary
rows.tip: If someone sends 100 at 0:59 and another 100 at 1:00, 200 requests get in within 2 seconds, and no rule has been broken.
The window moves with every moment, so there is no gap at the boundary as in a fixed window.

cells: Tokens accumulate, each request spends one
Handles bursts, keeps the average rate in check
You have to choose two numbers
rows.tip: The size of the bucket (how big a burst) and the refill rate (the average) are two separate numbers, and you have to think about both.

blocks.body: The refill speed sets the average rate, and the size of the bucket sets the burst. Two separate numbers.

aside.body: A small bucket means no bursts. A big bucket lets you save up and pour it all out at once.

items: For most public APIs token bucket is a good default: a user's natural bursts are tolerated.
Symfony's RateLimiter offers all three: fixed_window, sliding_window and token_bucket.

check.q: Why can twice the limit slip through at a fixed window's boundary?
check.a: Because the count resets to zero the moment the minute ends. 100 at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next means 200 within a few seconds.

slides.title: Adding a limit with Symfony RateLimiter
slides.tldr: Give a policy, limit and rate under framework.rate_limiter; in a listener, call consume() with the client's key; past the limit, throw TooManyRequestsHttpException.

blocks.body: First run `composer require symfony/rate-limiter`. Then declare a named limiter in the config. There, `limit` is the size of the bucket, and `rate` says how many tokens refill in what time. Keep the state somewhere all your app servers share, such as Redis, otherwise every server counts on its own.

blocks.code:
framework:
    cache:
        pools:
            rate_limiter_pool:
                adapter: cache.adapter.redis
    rate_limiter:
        api_per_client:
            policy: 'token_bucket'
            limit: 100
            rate: { interval: '1 minute', amount: 100 }
            cache_pool: 'rate_limiter_pool'

marks.tip: All app servers count in the same Redis. With a file cache, every server has its own count, and the limit effectively becomes 3 or 4 times higher.
limit: the size of the bucket, meaning at most 100 requests at once.
rate: 100 tokens flow back in every minute, so the average is 100 a minute.
The limiter is named api_per_client in the config, so the autowired argument is called $apiPerClientLimiter.
The key decides who is counted separately. Use a key you have checked (a known API key or the user id), else the IP. A header nobody verified can be invented anew on every request.
consume() tries to take one token. If the bucket is empty, isAccepted() is false.
This exception produces a response with a 429 and a Retry-After header.

items.desc: Check that the Redis env vars are right

items: An API key read from a header without checking it is not a safe key: a client can invent a new one on every request and get a fresh bucket each time. Look the key up first, or fall back to the IP.
Behind a load balancer without trusted_proxies, getClientIp() gives the same IP for everyone, and the limit blocks everybody at once.

items.label: trusted_proxies and the real client IP

check.q: With several app servers, why should the RateLimiter's state live somewhere shared, like Redis?
check.a: Otherwise every server counts on its own. With three servers the limit effectively triples, and a client can step over it easily.

slides.title: What a client does on a 429
slides.tldr: The server sends 429 and Retry-After. The client obeys that time, and if it is missing, retries with exponential backoff and jitter (a random delay).

blocks.body: If a client gets a 429 and sends again immediately, it makes the problem worse. The right behavior: if the server sends `Retry-After`, hold off for that long, and if not, double the wait each time. And if a thousand clients all retry at the same instant, the crowd comes back, so keep the wait random. That is called **jitter**.

blocks.caption: The maximum wait doubles on every attempt (with jitter the real wait is random between 0 and this)

items.label: Attempt 1
items.tip: After the first failure, any random delay between 0 and 1 second.

items.label: Attempt 2
items.tip: The second time, between 0 and 2 seconds.

items.label: Attempt 3
items.tip: The ceiling doubles each time, so the pressure on the server eases off gradually.

items.label: Attempt 5
items.tip: It grows up to a cap (say 30 seconds); after that it is better to give up and tell the user.

marks.tip: When the server tells you how long, obeying it is the most polite and correct thing to do. When it is a number of seconds, this is how to read it.
The wait grows 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds and is held at 30: exponential backoff.
Math.random() gives a random wait between 0 and the cap: jitter. A thousand clients then don't return at the same instant.

aside.title: Everyone came back at once
aside.body: A service went down for a minute, and thousands of clients came back together at exactly 1 second, 2 seconds and 4 seconds, knocking the service flat again and again. Without jitter, everyone's clocks tick in step.

items: Retry-After can also be an HTTP date, not just seconds. Handle both in production code.
Tell the user while they wait: "Trying again in a moment".

check.q: Why add jitter to backoff?
check.a: Without jitter, all the clients return at the same moment and make another crowd. Random delays spread them out, so the server can recover.

slides.title: Limit whom: IP, user or key
slides.tldr: Limit by IP and the thousand users of one mobile carrier count as one person. Use the user id or API key where you can, and a strict separate limit where it matters, like login.

blocks.body: On mobile data, thousands of users often come out of the same public IP. If you limit by IP alone, one person's fault blocks all their requests. On the other hand, with the user id alone you can't catch an attacker who hasn't logged in. So choose the key to suit the job.

blocks.caption: Choosing the key for a limit

rows.tip: With carrier NAT, offices or campuses, many people share one IP, so the limit has to be generous.
The fairest, because you count per person. But nobody has logged in yet at the login endpoint.

cells: If the key leaks, others use it
rows.tip: Each partner can get a separate limit and a separate quota. If one leaks, you only revoke that key.

cells: If it is the only one, the rest stays open
rows.tip: A separate strict limit on login to stop password guessing: for example 5 tries in 15 minutes.

blocks.code:
framework:
    rate_limiter:
        api_free:
            policy: 'token_bucket'
            limit: 30
            rate: { interval: '1 minute', amount: 30 }
        api_partner:
            policy: 'token_bucket'
            limit: 600
            rate: { interval: '1 minute', amount: 600 }
        login:
            policy: 'sliding_window'
            limit: 5
            interval: '15 minutes'

marks.tip: A small limit for users who don't pay.
A large limit for partners, as agreed in the contract. Each plan gets its own limiter.
A sliding window on login: no more than 5 in any 15-minute window. It stops brute force.
A prefix keeps user and IP counters apart. A person on mobile data is counted as themselves, not as the thousand people sharing their IP.
The email alone would let an attacker burn a victim's 5 tries. With the IP in the key, only the attacker's own bucket fills up.

blocks.body: A rate limit is the rate per minute; a quota is the total allowance for the month. You need both, and they are different things.

items: A quota is a separate thing: an allowance of 100,000 requests a month is usually kept in a database or Redis counter, not in the rate limiter.
Keep the error message safe: "too many attempts" is fine, "limit reached for this email" is not, because it reveals whether the email exists.
For login, turn on Symfony Security's `login_throttling` and you get much of this ready-made.
Price of a strict login limit: a real user who mistypes 5 times is locked out for 15 minutes. Show a clear message and a reset link.

check.q: Why does limiting by IP alone cause trouble for mobile-data users, and why does login get its own limit?
check.a: One carrier IP can hold thousands of people, so one person's fault blocks everyone. Login needs a separate strict limit to stop password guessing.

slides.title: The same phone, three prices
slides.tldr: If the discount or price calculation lives in the client's code, every client gives a different answer, and users can change that calculation themselves before sending it.

blocks.body: A phone costs $500, with a 10% discount running. On Ryan's website the discount calculation is in JavaScript, in the iOS app it is in separate code (by mistake it says 12%), and on the partner's site the calculation doesn't exist at all. In one month support got: "The website said $450, why does the partner's site say $500?" On top of that, one buyer opened DevTools, changed `total` to 1 cent and sent it, and the server accepted it.

blocks.caption: The price four clients show for the same cart

rows.tip: This calculation is correct, but it exists only in the web code. Nobody else knows about it.
A different developer, a different language, a different mistake. A fix takes days to get through the App Store.
It matches this time, but if the discount becomes 12% it must be changed in three places again, and one will be missed.
Your rules never reach an outside partner. They only see what the server returns.

blocks.body: A client is code in the user's hands. Don't believe what it says. Only what the server decided is true.

aside.title: The one-cent phone
aside.body: In a small e-commerce site, the checkout API trusted the `price` sent by the client. Someone set the price to 1 cent and ordered dozens of phones. There was no bug in the code, only trust placed in the wrong party.

items.meaning: The rules of the business: prices, discounts, who may do what, when something is canceled.
A client that makes no decisions of its own and only shows the server's decisions.

check.q: What goes wrong if the discount calculation is written separately for web, iOS and Android?
check.a: The three may show three prices, a rule change has to be made separately in all three, and users can alter the client's calculation and send it.

slides.title: The client shows, the server decides
slides.tldr: Business decisions (price, permissions, rules) are written once on the server. The client only shows the result and does small up-front checks for the user's convenience.

blocks.title: One store, three counters
blocks.body: The store has three checkout counters but only one price list, in the manager's office. The cashiers read the price from the list and announce it, instead of making it up in their heads. Add more counters and the prices still match, because the rules live in one place.

blocks.caption: Whose job is what

columns.title: Client (Vue, mobile)
items: Laying out results, language, dates, money formatting
Up-front convenience checks: does the email contain @
Showing or hiding buttons from a flag the server sent
columns.tip: The screen in front of the user. Its job is to show things quickly and nicely, not to make decisions.

columns.title: Server (Symfony)
items: Calculating price, discount and tax
Who may do what: permissions
The real validation, stock and all business rules
columns.tip: The place where the real decisions are made. Everyone gets the same answer from here.

blocks.body: Client checks are for convenience, server checks are for security. Nothing is final unless the server says so.

aside.body: The client shows, the server decides.

use: Keep in the client: layout, animation, up-front form checks, cached UI state
avoid: Don't keep in the client: price, discount, permissions, stock, payment rules

items.label: Why validation on the server is mandatory

check.q: The email field already has an up-front check in the client. Why validate again on the server?
check.a: A client check is only a convenience. Anyone calling the API directly or changing the code skips it, so the real check has to be on the server.

slides.title: The server builds the price, the client only sends items
slides.tldr: The client sends only the product id and quantity. The server works out the price, discount and total from its own database and returns them.

blocks.body: In the old code the client sent `total` and `discount`, and the server stored them as they were. Turn that around: the client only says what it wants to buy, and the server calculates using the real prices in the database. The calculation goes back in the response, so the client only displays it.

marks.tip: Change total in DevTools and 1 cent goes straight in here. The server verifies nothing.
The size of the discount is decided by the user too. Anyone can take any discount.
The price comes from the database, not from what the client says. An unknown product throws an exception.
In cents (whole numbers). Keep money in floats and fraction errors pile up.
The discount rule lives in one place, DiscountPolicy. To go from 10% to 12%, touch only this.

items: The controller just takes `#[MapRequestPayload] CreateOrderRequest` and calls PriceCalculator. No calculation in the controller.
Return `subtotal`, `discount` and `total` in the response, so the client doesn't calculate at all, it only shows.
Always keep money in whole numbers (cents), never floats.

check.q: In a checkout API, what does the client send and what doesn't it, and who calculates the price?
check.a: The client sends the product id and quantity. It does not send total or discount. The server calculates the price from the real prices in the database and its own rules.

slides.title: Checkout end to end: the tampered total is ignored
slides.tldr: The controller reads only product ids and quantities, gets a Quote from PriceCalculator, saves it and returns the numbers; a total changed in DevTools is never read.

blocks.body: Now the same phone, end to end. The request class declares only `items`, so an extra `total` in the JSON has nowhere to land. The controller asks `PriceCalculator` for a `Quote`, saves it and returns the numbers for the client to display.

marks.tip: CreateOrderRequest holds only the list of items (product id and quantity). A total or discount in the JSON is never read.
Every number comes from this quote, built from the database prices.
The client displays this total. It never works it out.

blocks.caption: The $500 phone, with a tampered request

rows.tip: The user changed total to 1 in DevTools. The request still carries it.
The product's real price, 50,000 cents, from the products table.
The rule lives in one class on the server.
The 1 cent sent by the client was never read, so it cannot be stored.

items: Price: the client can no longer show a total instantly while the user changes quantity. Add a quote endpoint that calls the same PriceCalculator, and show the last quote while it loads.
Prices can change between the quote and the order, so the order must be built from a fresh quote, never from the one the client saw earlier.

check.q: The JSON says `total: 1`, but the controller above stores $450. Why?
check.a: The request class has no `total`, and the order is built from a Quote the server calculated from the database prices and DiscountPolicy.

slides.title: Who decides whether to show the button
slides.tldr: The permission rule lives on the server (a Voter). Send `abilities` flags in the response and the client shows or hides buttons from them; the server checks again on the real action.

blocks.body: When should the "Cancel order" button show? If you write `if (order.status === 'placed' && order.owner === me)` in Vue, the rule has now been written a second time, and when you change it in one place the other stays out of date. Better to let the server decide with a Voter, and say in the response "this user can do this".

marks.tip: The decision is made by calling the same Voter. The client gets only the result, not the rule.
The real cancel uses the same Voter too. Whatever the client's flag says, the server checks again.

blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
defineProps<{ order: { id: number; abilities: { cancel: boolean } } }>()
const emit = defineEmits<{ cancel: [id: number] }>()
</script>

<template>
  <button v-if="order.abilities.cancel" @click="emit('cancel', order.id)">
    Cancel order
  </button>
</template>

marks.tip: v-if only looks at the server's flag. When the rule changes, the client's code doesn't have to.

items: Hiding a button with a flag is not security, only good UX. If the real action's endpoint has no permission check, anyone can call the API directly.
When the permission rule changes, say "canceling is allowed for 1 hour even after shipping", change the server's Voter; the client stays untouched.
A flag can be stale: the order may ship a minute after the page loaded. The real action's 403 is the final word, so show a clear message when it comes.
In a list of 50 orders the Voter runs 50 times. Keep it cheap and load what it needs once.

check.q: Is the permission job done once the button is hidden in Vue? Why, or why not?
check.a: No. Hiding is only UX. Anyone can call the endpoint directly, so the server must check again with #[IsGranted].

slides.title: BFF: the shape changes, not the rules
slides.tldr: A Backend for Frontend joins and trims data to fit each client's screen. The business rules still stay in the core server, not in the BFF.

blocks.body: The web and mobile screens differ, so the shape of the data they need differs too. You can put a thin server in front of each client, called a BFF. It calls the core services and builds a single response that fits the screen. But it only changes the shape: the decisions about price or permissions stay in the core services.

blocks.title: What belongs in a BFF, and what doesn't
items: Belongs: calling several services and building one response, trimming and arranging data
Belongs: client-specific shape and language-related formatting
Doesn't belong: price, discount, permissions, cancellation rules

use: Web and mobile screens really differ, and different teams build them
avoid: When there is only one client. You'd be running an extra server for nothing
When you put business rules in the BFF. The rules get duplicated in two places again

check.q: What goes wrong if you keep the discount calculation in a BFF?
check.a: Every BFF ends up with its own copy of the calculation, and the "three prices in three places" problem comes right back. The rules should stay in the core service.
